paragraphs.heading: Who he was
paragraphs.text: Harry Hammond Hess was an American geologist who lived from 1906 to 1969 and served as an officer in the United States Navy during World War II. Plate tectonics is a unifying theory, and he is considered one of its founding fathers. He published theories on sea floor spreading and suggested that what drives the process is convection in the Earth's mantle.

paragraphs.heading: An unpromising start
paragraphs.text: Hess was born in New York City on May 24, 1906, and entered Yale University in 1923. His plan was to study electrical engineering, but the Bachelor of Science degree he graduated with was in geology. The first time he took mineralogy at Yale he failed, and he was told that the field held no future for him. He carried on with his degree anyway. He also worked for two years in Northern Rhodesia as an exploration geologist, and he joined the Princeton University faculty in 1934. He stayed at Princeton for the rest of his career and chaired its Geology Department from 1950 to 1966.

paragraphs.heading: A warship as a survey vessel
paragraphs.text: During World War II Hess joined the United States Navy and became captain of an attack transport ship, the USS Cape Johnson. The ship carried sonar, which was a new technology. Hess tracked his routes carefully on the way to Pacific Ocean landings on the Marianas, the Philippines and Iwo Jima, and used the ship's echo sounder continuously. This unplanned surveying let him collect profiles of the ocean floor across the North Pacific Ocean. It led to the discovery of flat-topped submarine volcanoes. He named them guyots, for Arnold Henry Guyot, a geographer of the 19th century.

paragraphs.heading: The 1960 report
paragraphs.text: In 1960 Hess made his single most important contribution. It is regarded as one part of the 20th century's major advance in geologic science. In a report to the Office of Naval Research that was widely circulated, he proposed that the Earth's crust moves sideways, away from long oceanic ridges that are volcanically active. That theory is now generally accepted. His wartime command later proved key to developing it. Even so, he only understood his North Pacific profiles after Marie Tharp and Bruce Heezen discovered the Great Global Rift, which runs along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

paragraphs.heading: What the idea changed
paragraphs.text: The process Hess described was later named seafloor spreading. Alfred Wegener's earlier concept of continental drift had been generally dismissed at the time. Seafloor spreading helped establish it as scientifically respectable, and this set off a revolution in the earth sciences. Hess's report was formally published in 1962 in his History of Ocean Basins. For a time, no work in solid-earth geophysics was referenced more.

paragraphs.heading: Later work and honours
paragraphs.text: After the war Hess stayed in the Naval Reserve and rose to the rank of rear admiral. He was also involved in the Mohole project of 1957 to 1966, which looked into the feasibility and techniques of deep sea drilling. The United States National Academy of Sciences elected him in 1952. In 1963 he presided over The Geological Society of America, which gave him its Penrose Medal in 1966. On August 25, 1969, he died of a heart attack in Woods Hole, Massachusetts. In 1984 the American Geophysical Union established a medal in his memory that carries his name.
